title: The New Kingdom
subtitle: 1550–1200 BC · Empire, the Amarna Rupture and the Ramesside Recovery

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: From Ahmose's expulsion of the Hyksos through the Thutmosid conquests, the Amarna rupture and the Ramesside recovery to Merneptah

entries.label: Ahmose I — the expulsion of the Hyksos
entries.hint: Ahmose I completed the war his father Seqenenre and brother Kamose had fought: he took Avaris, chased the Hyksos into southern Canaan and besieged them at Sharuhen, then turned south to break a Nubian revolt. Egypt was one kingdom again for the first time in a century and a half, and the reign is conventionally the start of the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom. The soldier Ahmose son of Ibana of el-Kab left the fullest eyewitness account.
entries.note: Autobiography of Ahmose son of Ibana, tomb at el-Kab: translation Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976) pp.12–15. Tell el-Dab'a (Avaris) end-of-Hyksos horizon: Bietak, Avaris (1996). Shaw (ed.), Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000) pp.207–14.

entries.label: Amenhotep I — consolidation and the necropolis founded
entries.hint: Amenhotep I ruled a peaceful, consolidating reign, campaigning only lightly in Nubia and Libya. He and his mother Ahmose-Nefertari were later worshipped for centuries as the patron gods of the Theban west bank and are the traditional founders of the workmen's village at Deir el-Medina. His tomb has never been securely identified, and he may have been the first king to separate tomb from mortuary temple, the pattern the Valley of the Kings then followed.
entries.note: Deir el-Medina cult of Amenhotep I and Ahmose-Nefertari: Jaroslav Černý, A Community of Workmen at Thebes in the Ramesside Period (1973). The Abbott and other Ramesside tomb-robbery papyri place his tomb intact in their day. Shaw (2000) pp.218–20.

entries.label: Thutmose I — to the Euphrates and past the Fourth Cataract
entries.hint: Thutmose I, of non-royal birth, campaigned further in both directions than any Egyptian king before him: south beyond the Fourth Cataract, where a boundary stela at Tombos records the crushing of Kush, and north across Syria to the Euphrates, where he set up a stela on the 'inverted water that runs backwards'. He is also the first king with a securely identified tomb in the Valley of the Kings.
entries.note: Tombos stela (year 2) and the Euphrates campaign: Urkunden IV (Sethe) 82–103; Redford, Egypt, Canaan, and Israel in Ancient Times (1992) pp.148–51. Tomb KV38 (and KV20, shared with Hatshepsut): Reeves & Wilkinson, The Complete Valley of the Kings (1996).

entries.label: Thutmose II — a short reign and a Nubian revolt
entries.hint: Thutmose II, son of Thutmose I by a secondary wife, reigned only a few years. An Aswan inscription records his army suppressing a revolt in Kush with orders to kill every male. He married his fully royal half-sister Hatshepsut; their daughter was Neferure, and the future Thutmose III was his son by a lesser wife, Isis. His mummy shows a man dead in his thirties.
entries.note: Aswan/Sehel inscription of the Kush revolt: Urkunden IV 137–41. Reign length debated (3–13 years); Luc Gabolde, 'La chronologie du règne de Thoutmosis II', SAK 14 (1987). Mummy (Cairo CG 61066), Deir el-Bahari cache.

entries.label: Hatshepsut — the woman who ruled as king
entries.hint: Hatshepsut began as regent for her infant stepson Thutmose III and within about seven years had taken the full kingly titulary and male regalia, ruling roughly two decades of prosperity and building. Her terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari, her pair of Karnak obelisks and the reliefs of her trading expedition to Punt are among the period's masterworks. Late in Thutmose III's reign her name and images were systematically hacked from many monuments — a delayed act, probably about succession legitimacy rather than personal spite.
entries.note: Deir el-Bahari (Djeser-djeseru): excavated by Naville (EEF) and the Metropolitan Museum; Polish–Egyptian restoration since 1961. The proscription's late date: Charles Nims, 'The Date of the Dishonoring of Hatshepsut', ZÄS 93 (1966); Roehrig (ed.), Hatshepsut: From Queen to Pharaoh (2005).

entries.label: Thutmose III — the empire at its greatest extent
entries.hint: Once he ruled alone, Thutmose III led at least seventeen campaigns into the Levant across twenty years, opening with the victory at Megiddo, breaking the Mitanni-backed coalition of Syrian princes, and crossing the Euphrates to raid Mitannian territory. Egypt's empire reached from the Fourth Cataract of the Nile to northern Syria. His campaign annals, carved on the walls at Karnak from the daybook of the army, are the fullest military record of the ancient Near East.
entries.note: Annals of Thutmose III, Karnak: Urkunden IV 645–756; translation in Redford, The Wars in Syria and Palestine of Thutmose III (2003). Empire overview: Shaw (2000) pp.238–48.

entries.label: Amenhotep II — holding the empire by fear
entries.hint: Amenhotep II advertised his own strength — a stela at Giza claims no one could draw his bow — and put down Syrian resistance with calculated brutality: his campaign stelae record bringing home the bodies of seven princes of Takhsy hung head-down from the prow of his ship, six then displayed on the walls of Thebes and one sent to Napata as a warning. After his reign the northern empire settled into a stable frontier with Mitanni.
entries.note: Memphis and Karnak stelae of Amenhotep II: Urkunden IV 1281–1315; translation in Pritchard (ed.), Ancient Near Eastern Texts (ANET, 1969) pp.245–48. Der Manuelian, Studies in the Reign of Amenophis II (1987).

entries.label: Thutmose IV — the Dream Stele and peace with Mitanni
entries.hint: Thutmose IV set a granite stela between the paws of the Great Sphinx recording a dream in which the sun god promised him the throne if he cleared the sand from the monument — a legitimising story for a king who may not have been the designated heir. His reign ended the long cold war with Mitanni by marriage: he took a daughter of King Artatama I as a wife, the first of several such Egyptian–Mitannian royal marriages.
entries.note: Dream Stele, Giza: Urkunden IV 1539–44; Zivie-Coche, Sphinx: History of a Monument (2002). Mitanni marriage: the Amarna letters (EA 29) refer back to it; Betsy Bryan, The Reign of Thutmose IV (1991).

entries.label: Amenhotep III — the reign of magnificence
entries.hint: Amenhotep III ruled nearly forty years of peace and unmatched wealth, fed by Nubian gold and Levantine tribute. He built on a colossal scale — the Luxor temple, the largest-ever mortuary temple behind the Colossi of Memnon, the Malkata palace-city, a temple at Soleb in Nubia — issued series of commemorative scarabs recording his marriages, lion hunts and a pleasure lake dug in fifteen days, and corresponded as an equal with the kings of Babylon, Mitanni and Arzawa. Late in the reign he promoted the sun-disc, the Aten, as a special royal cult.
entries.note: Commemorative scarabs: Blankenberg-van Delden, The Large Commemorative Scarabs of Amenhotep III (1969). Malkata and the mortuary temple: Kozloff & Bryan (eds.), Egypt's Dazzling Sun: Amenhotep III and his World (1992). Amarna letters from his reign: Moran, The Amarna Letters (1992).

entries.label: Akhenaten — the Aten and the abandoned capital
entries.hint: Amenhotep IV changed his name to Akhenaten, declared the sun-disc Aten the sole god, built a new capital, Akhetaten, on virgin ground in Middle Egypt, and eventually closed the temples of Amun and had the god's name chiselled out across Egypt. Court art broke every convention — elongated bodies, intimate family scenes, the king shown with his queen Nefertiti as near-equals. Cuneiform letters from vassals and allies pile up unanswered while the empire's northern grip loosened.
entries.note: Boundary stelae of Akhetaten: Murnane & Van Siclen, The Boundary Stelae of Akhenaten (1993). Amarna letters: William L. Moran, The Amarna Letters (1992). Surveys: Dodson, Amarna Sunrise (2014); Barry Kemp, The City of Akhenaten and Nefertiti: Amarna and its People (2012).

entries.label: Neferneferuaten and Smenkhkare — the contested succession
entries.hint: Akhenaten's last years and immediate aftermath are the murkiest in Egyptian royal history. A co-ruler using the throne name Ankhkheperure appears — under the name Neferneferuaten (with feminine grammar in some writings, so probably Nefertiti or a royal daughter ruling as king) and, separately or successively, as a male Smenkhkare. Within a few years all were gone and the child Tutankhaten held the throne.
entries.note: The 'Coregency Stela' (recut), Amarna letters EA dating, and the KV55 burial. Competing reconstructions: James Allen, 'The Amarna Succession', in Brand & Cooper (eds.), Causing His Name to Live (2009); Aidan Dodson, Amarna Sunset (2009); Marc Gabolde, D'Akhenaton à Toutânkhamon (1998).

entries.label: Tutankhamun — the restoration of the old gods
entries.hint: Tutankhaten came to the throne at about nine, changed his name to Tutankhamun, abandoned Amarna, and issued a Restoration Stela describing the land as neglected and the gods' shrines fallen, and himself as putting it right — the work in practice of the courtiers Ay and Horemheb. He died at eighteen or nineteen with no surviving heir. His near-intact tomb, found by Howard Carter in 1922, made him the most famous of all Egyptian kings despite a minor reign.
entries.note: Restoration Stela (Cairo CG 34183), from Karnak: Urkunden IV 2025–32. Tomb KV62: Carter & Mace, The Tomb of Tut·ankh·Amen (1923–33); Reeves, The Complete Tutankhamun (1990). CT/DNA study of the mummy: Hawass et al., JAMA 303 (2010).

entries.label: Ay — the courtier who buried the king and took the throne
entries.hint: Ay, an elderly 'god's father' who had been a senior figure since Akhenaten's reign and probably Nefertiti's relative, performed the Opening of the Mouth ritual at Tutankhamun's funeral — shown doing so on the tomb wall, in kingly dress — and then reigned about four years himself. A letter from Tutankhamun's widow to the Hittite king asking for a prince to marry, which ended with the prince murdered en route, is usually read against this succession.
entries.note: Ay in KV62's burial-chamber painting; his own tomb WV23. The 'Dahamunzu affair': the Hittite 'Deeds of Suppiluliuma' (Güterbock, JCS 10, 1956); identification of the widow debated (Ankhesenamun most likely). Schneider, 'The Hittite–Egyptian correspondence', in various.

entries.label: Horemheb — the general who reset the state
entries.hint: Horemheb, army commander and 'deputy of the king' under Tutankhamun, took the throne without royal blood and governed as a restorer: a Great Edict (preserved at Karnak) against official corruption and abuse of the poor, the dismantling of the Amarna temples for fill in his own pylons, and the writing of Akhenaten, Neferneferuaten, Tutankhamun and Ay out of the king-lists so that his own reign followed straight on from Amenhotep III. Childless, he named his vizier and general Paramessu as heir.
entries.note: Great Edict of Horemheb, Karnak: Urkunden IV 2140–62; Kruchten, Le Décret d'Horemheb (1981). His Memphite (pre-royal) tomb at Saqqara and royal tomb KV57: Martin, The Memphite Tomb of Horemheb (1989).

entries.label: Ramesses I — the founder from the army
entries.hint: Paramessu, a career soldier and vizier from a military family of the eastern Delta, became Ramesses I on Horemheb's death, already old. He reigned little more than a year — long enough to begin the great hypostyle hall at Karnak and to raise his son Seti to co-regent — and is the founder of the Nineteenth Dynasty, the Ramesside line.
entries.note: Tomb KV16. Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions I; Kitchen, Pharaoh Triumphant: The Life and Times of Ramesses II (1982) pp.15–18. His mummy, taken to North America in the 19th c., was returned to Egypt in 2003.

entries.label: Seti I — the recovery of the empire
entries.hint: Seti I set out to win back what had slipped since Amarna: campaign reliefs on the north wall of the Karnak hypostyle hall show him retaking Canaan, striking the Hittites' Syrian clients, and a clash with the Hittite army near Kadesh. At home he built the finely carved Abydos temple with its king-list, completed much of the Karnak hall, and cut the largest and most elaborately decorated tomb in the Valley of the Kings, KV17.
entries.note: Karnak war reliefs: The Epigraphic Survey, The Battle Reliefs of King Sety I (1986). Abydos temple and king-list: Calverley & Broome, The Temple of King Sethos I at Abydos (1933–58). KV17: Reeves & Wilkinson, The Complete Valley of the Kings (1996).

entries.label: Ramesses II — sixty-six years and the Hittite peace
entries.hint: Ramesses II reigned about sixty-six years, the defining Ramesside reign. Year 5 brought the near-disaster and claimed victory at Kadesh against the Hittites; Year 21, a sworn peace treaty with Hatti, later sealed by his marriage to a Hittite princess. He moved the capital to a new city, Pi-Ramesses, in his Delta homeland, and built more than any other king — Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum, additions at Karnak, Luxor, Abydos and Memphis, and colossal statues everywhere, fathering perhaps a hundred children.
entries.note: Kitchen, Pharaoh Triumphant: The Life and Times of Ramesses II (1982); Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions II. Pi-Ramesses (Qantir/Tell el-Dab'a): Pusch & Herold, magnetometer survey, Ägypten und Levante (1990s). Tomb KV7; his mummy, Cairo.

entries.label: Merneptah — the Libyan war and the Israel Stele
entries.hint: Merneptah, already elderly as Ramesses II's thirteenth son and long-serving crown prince, faced in his fifth year a large invasion of the western Delta by a Libyan king allied with northern sea-raiders — Ekwesh, Shekelesh, Lukka, Sherden, Teresh. He defeated it in a six-hour battle and recorded the victory at Karnak and on a stela that lists his subdued enemies, including the earliest known written mention of Israel, 'laid waste, its seed is not'.
entries.note: Great Karnak Inscription and the 'Israel Stela' (Cairo JE 31408, reused from Amenhotep III): translation in ANET pp.376–78; Manfred Görg and the 'Israel' debate, e.g. Michael Hasel, Domination and Resistance (1998). Colleen Manassa, The Great Karnak Inscription of Merneptah (2003).

entries.label: The disputed end of the Nineteenth Dynasty
entries.hint: After Merneptah the dynasty fractured: his son Seti II held the throne against a rival, Amenmesse, who ruled the south for a few years; then the boy-king Siptah under the powerful chancellor Bay, a foreigner later executed on the king's order; and finally Seti II's widow Tawosret as sole female king. Setnakhte seized power around 1189 and founded the Twentieth Dynasty, remembering the preceding years — in the later Great Harris Papyrus — as a time when 'Egypt was in the hands of chiefs and rulers of towns'.
entries.note: Amenmesse: Rolf Krauss and Frank Yurco's competing reconstructions. Bay's execution: Ostracon IFAO 1864 (Grandet, BIFAO 100, 2000). Tawosret's tomb KV14. Retrospective: Great Harris Papyrus (P. BM EA 9999); Grandet, Le papyrus Harris I (1994). This coda's later phase runs just past this folio's close.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Syrian and Nubian wars of empire, Megiddo and Kadesh, and the first Libyan and Sea Peoples raids

entries.label: Ahmose takes Avaris and Sharuhen
entries.hint: Ahmose I's forces stormed the Hyksos capital Avaris and then pursued the survivors into southwest Canaan, besieging them for three years at Sharuhen before taking it. The soldier Ahmose son of Ibana, rewarded with 'gold of valour' and captives after each action, describes fighting on the water at Avaris and the fall of Sharuhen in his tomb autobiography — the campaign that ended a century of foreign rule in the north.
entries.note: Autobiography of Ahmose son of Ibana, el-Kab; Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976) pp.12–15. Avaris destruction horizon: Bietak, Avaris (1996). Sharuhen usually located at Tell el-Ajjul or Tell el-Far'ah (South).

entries.label: The conquest of Kush to the Fourth Cataract
entries.hint: Across the first century of the New Kingdom, Egypt turned Nubia from a raided frontier into an annexed province. Ahmose and Amenhotep I broke the early revolts, Thutmose I pushed the border past the Fourth Cataract with the Tombos stela, and Thutmose III fixed Napata, below Gebel Barkal, as the southern limit. Temple-towns at Soleb, Sesebi and Sai and a settled Egyptian administration replaced the fortresses, and Nubian gold became the empire's financial backbone.
entries.note: Tombos stela: Urkunden IV 82–86. Nubian temple-towns: Morris, The Architecture of Imperialism (2005); Stuart Tyson Smith, Wretched Kush (2003). Napata frontier: Kendall, 'Gebel Barkal', in various.

entries.label: The Battle of Megiddo
entries.hint: In his twenty-third year Thutmose III marched against a coalition of Canaanite and Syrian princes led by the ruler of Kadesh and backed by Mitanni, gathered at Megiddo. Against his officers' advice he took the army single-file through the narrow Aruna pass and emerged unopposed on the plain. The enemy broke at the first clash but the Egyptians stopped to loot, and the city held out through a seven-month siege before surrendering — the earliest battle in history recorded in tactical detail.
entries.note: Annals of Thutmose III, Karnak (the 'Gebel Barkal' and Armant stelae supplement): Urkunden IV 647–67; Redford, The Wars in Syria and Palestine of Thutmose III (2003) pp.7–36. Analysis: Cline, The Battles of Armageddon (2000).

entries.label: Thutmose III breaks Mitanni's coalition
entries.hint: Over sixteen further campaigns Thutmose III dismantled Mitanni's influence in Syria: he took the ports of the Levantine coast to supply his army by sea, stormed the inland strongholds, and in his thirty-third year crossed the Euphrates on boats carried overland from Byblos to raid Mitannian territory and set up a stela beside his grandfather's. He hunted 120 elephants in the marshes of Niya on the way home. The northern empire he left ran to the Orontes and beyond.
entries.note: Annals, Urkunden IV 689–734; the Gebel Barkal Stela (Boston MFA 23.733) on the Euphrates crossing and the elephant hunt. Redford, The Wars in Syria and Palestine of Thutmose III (2003).

entries.label: Amenhotep II's campaigns of terror
entries.hint: Amenhotep II campaigned twice in Syria early in his reign, and his stelae dwell on cruelty as policy: he personally killed seven rebel princes of the district of Takhsy, brought their bodies back hanging head-down from his ship's prow, and had six hung on the enclosure wall of Thebes and the seventh sent upriver to be displayed at Napata 'to make manifest the victories of the king forever'. After this the Syrian frontier stabilised and formal peace with Mitanni followed under his son.
entries.note: Memphis and Karnak stelae of Amenhotep II: Urkunden IV 1288–1309; ANET pp.245–48. Der Manuelian, Studies in the Reign of Amenophis II (1987) pp.62–91.

entries.label: The Battle of Kadesh
entries.hint: In his fifth year Ramesses II marched on Kadesh and was fed false intelligence that the Hittite army under Muwatalli II was far to the north. His four divisions strung out, and Hittite chariots ambushed the second as it made camp, scattering it and nearly overrunning the king. Ramesses rallied with his guard and a relief column arriving from the coast until the Hittites withdrew into the city. Egypt held the field but not the objective; both sides claimed victory, and Ramesses covered temple walls with the story in a 'Poem', a 'Bulletin' and battle reliefs.
entries.note: The Kadesh texts: Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions II 2–147; translation Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions Translated II (1996). The Hittite side: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005) pp.234–41. Murnane, The Road to Kadesh (2nd ed. 1990).

entries.label: The Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty
entries.hint: Sixteen years after Kadesh, Ramesses II and Hattusili III swore a treaty of permanent peace, non-aggression, mutual defence against attack and against internal revolt, and the extradition of fugitives, with the gods of both lands as witnesses. It survives as an Egyptian version carved at Karnak and the Ramesseum and as Akkadian cuneiform tablets from the Hittite capital — the only ancient international treaty preserved from both parties, and the model for a plaque at the United Nations.
entries.note: Egyptian version: Kitchen, Ramesside Inscriptions II 225–32. Hittite (Akkadian) tablets from Hattusa: Edel, Der Vertrag zwischen Ramses II. und Hattušili III. (1997). The treaty is dated to Ramesses II's Year 21.

entries.label: Merneptah's Libyan war
entries.hint: In Merneptah's fifth year the Libyan king Merey led his people, with their households and cattle, into the western Delta alongside allied sea-raiders — Ekwesh, Shekelesh, Lukka, Sherden and Teresh, some of the earliest 'Sea Peoples' named. Egyptian forces met and destroyed them at a place called Perire, killing some six thousand and taking thousands of prisoners; Merey fled. It was the first of the great western and northern assaults that would define the end of the Bronze Age.
entries.note: Great Karnak Inscription of Merneptah: Manassa, The Great Karnak Inscription of Merneptah (2003); the Athribis and Cairo 'Israel' stelae supplement. Cline, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (2014) pp.1–10, 121–28 on the wider context.
